title: Martin Luther King Jr.: The Letter from Birmingham Jail — 1963
summary: Confined inside a dark cell in Birmingham, Alabama, in April 1963, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. penned his immortal manifesto: 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere'.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 189: காந்தியின் நகைச்சுவை: “சிரிப்பு இல்லையெனில் தாக்குதல்கள் என்னைக் கொன்றிருக்கும்”
full_text:
In April 1963, Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was arrested in Birmingham, Alabama, for defying an injunction against peaceful civil rights demonstrations in what was then the most segregated city in America.

Confined in solitary darkness without a mattress or writing desk, King read an open letter in a local newspaper authored by eight moderate white clergymen urging the Black community to cease street demonstrations and 'wait' patiently for gradual courtroom remedies.

Using the margins of the newspaper and scraps of paper smuggled by his lawyer, King drafted the legendary 'Letter from Birmingham Jail':

"My dear fellow clergymen,
You deplore the demonstrations taking place in Birmingham. But your statement, I am sorry to say, fails to express a similar concern for the conditions that brought about the demonstrations. For years now I have heard the word 'Wait!' It rings in the ear of every Negro with piercing familiarity. This 'Wait' has almost always meant 'Never.' Justice too long delayed is justice denied.

You ask why I came to Birmingham. I am here because injustice is here!
Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere. We are caught in an inescapable network of mutuality, tied in a single garment of destiny. Whatever affects one directly, affects all indirectly!
One who breaks an unjust law that conscience tells him is contrary to the law of God, and who willingly accepts the penalty of imprisonment in order to arouse the conscience of the community over its injustice, is in reality expressing the highest respect for law!"

King's letter became one of the greatest moral manifestos in world history, establishing the sacred duty of non-violent resistance against systemic oppression.
